extracted_claims.text: AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection of natural persons are listed as high-risk under Annex III, point 4 of the AI Act.
A 'deployer' is defined under Article 3(4) as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except in purely personal non-professional use.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III that make or assist in decisions about natural persons must inform those persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system (Article 26(11)).
Under Article 26(5), deployers of high-risk AI systems must monitor the system's operation based on the provider's instructions for use and must inform the provider of any serious incidents.

Article 27 requires a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) prior to first deployment, but only for deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, or deployers of Annex III points 5(b) and (c); general private-sector employers deploying hiring tools (Annex III point 4) are not explicitly named in this list.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must complete a conformity assessment (Articles 8-15, 43), issue an EU Declaration of Conformity (Article 47), affix CE marking (Article 48), and register the system in the EU database (Article 49).

Market surveillance authorities may evaluate AI systems that providers misclassified as non-high-risk to circumvent Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and impose fines under Article 99 if misclassification is established.

The AI Act establishes national procedures (Articles 74, 79, 80) and penalty provisions (Chapter XII, Articles 99-101) for market surveillance and non-compliance of AI systems, including high-risk systems.
Penalties for non-compliance with high-risk AI obligations can reach €15 million (or a percentage of global turnover, per secondary reporting).

Industry guides recommend deployer compliance steps such as AI tool inventories, DPIAs/FRIAs, human oversight roles, logging and record-retention, bias analysis, AI literacy training, and candidate explanation processes ahead of enforcement deadlines.
Some sources state that full compliance for high-risk AI obligations, including hiring tools, is required by 2 August 2026.

A source referencing an 'Omnibus' legislative update states that high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III systems (including hiring) have been deferred to 2 December 2027, with Annex I embedded high-risk systems deferred to 2 August 2028, and that these dates are fixed and not conditional on further Commission decisions.
The European Commission missed its February 2026 guidance deadline related to AI Act implementation, which one source says creates interpretive risk but not a compliance extension.
Under Italian Garante guidance, companies using AI for recruitment must perform a specialized DPIA addressing algorithmic bias and satisfy transparency requirements under both GDPR and the AI Act.
The Italian Garante fined OpenAI/ChatGPT approximately €15-15.58 million for GDPR violations.
The Italian Garante fined Clearview AI €20 million in February 2022 for unlawful biometric data processing of Italian residents, ordering data deletion and an EU representative designation.
The Italian Garante imposed an urgent limitation on DeepSeek's processing of Italian users' personal data in January 2025 over data protection concerns.

report:
# Compliance Requirements and Enforcement for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
AI recruitment and selection tools are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act, triggering obligations for both providers (conformity assessment, CE marking, registration) and deployers (monitoring, transparency to candidates) (high confidence). However, significant uncertainty remains around the applicable compliance deadline, the scope of Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment obligations for private employers, and whether any enforcement actions have actually occurred under the AI Act itself as opposed to GDPR.

## Key Findings

### Classification and Scope
AI systems used for recruitment or selection of natural persons are explicitly listed as high-risk under Annex III, point 4 of the AI Act (high confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/office-has-become-diy-ai-lab-who-checking-what-goes-and-what-comes-out), [ANNEX III](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3)). A "deployer" is defined under Article 3(4) as any natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or body using an AI system under its authority, excluding purely personal non-professional use — meaning most employers using hiring AI qualify (medium confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/office-has-become-diy-ai-lab-who-checking-what-goes-and-what-comes-out)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers of high-risk AI systems must complete a conformity assessment, issue an EU Declaration of Conformity, affix CE marking, and register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market (high confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment), [Resemble AI](https://www.resemble.ai/resources/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-ai-companies), [AI Act Service Desk, Art. 48](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-48)).

### Deployer Obligations
Deployers must inform individuals subject to high-risk AI decisions that such a system is being used (Article 26(11)) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26)). Deployers are also required to monitor system operation per the provider's instructions and report serious incidents, though this claim carries low confidence due to limited corroboration (low confidence) ([EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf)). A Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) is required under Article 27 before first deployment, but the text appears to limit this obligation to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and certain Annex III categories (5(b)/(c)) — general private-sector employers deploying hiring tools under Annex III point 4 are not explicitly named (high confidence) ([European Parliament study](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf), [AI Act Service Desk, Art. 27](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-27)). Industry guides nonetheless recommend broader deployer practices—tool inventories, DPIAs/FRIAs, human oversight, logging, bias analysis, staff AI literacy training, and candidate explanation processes—though these recommendations carry low confidence as interpretive, non-authoritative guidance ([Khairos](https://www.khairos.ai/blog/comply/eu-ai-act-for-hr-managers-2026-guide), [Ninjahire](https://ninjahire.co/thoughts/eu-ai-act-hiring-explained), [RegulatoryAI](https://www.regulatoryai.eu/ai-act-compliance-checklist)).

### Timelines
Sources conflict on the compliance deadline: some state full high-risk obligations, including for hiring tools, apply from 2 August 2026 (low confidence) ([Khairos](https://www.khairos.ai/blog/comply/eu-ai-act-for-hr-managers-2026-guide), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/high-risk-ai-systems-eu-ai-act-guide)), while another source claims an "Omnibus" legislative update deferred stand-alone Annex III obligations (including hiring) to 2 December 2027 (low confidence) ([SIG](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/eu-ai-act-summary)). One source also notes the European Commission missed a February 2026 guidance deadline, creating interpretive uncertainty but not a formal extension (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/high-risk-ai-systems-eu-ai-act-guide)).

### Enforcement Mechanisms and Penalties
The AI Act establishes national market surveillance procedures and penalty provisions under Articles 74, 79, 80, and 99–101 for non-compliance, including misclassification of high-risk systems to evade obligations (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 74](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-74), [Art. 99](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-99), [Art. 80](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-80)). A secondary source cites penalties of up to €15 million or a percentage of global turnover, but this figure is low confidence and not confirmed by primary legal text ([Khairos](https://www.khairos.ai/blog/comply/eu-ai-act-for-hr-managers-2026-guide)).

### Related Enforcement (GDPR, not AI Act)
No AI Act enforcement action against a hiring-tool provider or deployer has been documented. The Italian Garante has fined OpenAI roughly €15 million under GDPR (medium confidence) ([Legal500](https://www.legal500.com/intelligence/italy/privacy/laws-guidance-and-recommendations-what-to-consider-when-using-ai-to-hire-employees-in-italy)), fined Clearview AI €20 million in 2022 for biometric data violations (low confidence) ([GDPRFine.com](https://gdprfine.com/dpa/italy-garante)), and restricted DeepSeek's processing of Italian users' data in 2025 (low confidence) ([Regulations.AI](https://regulations.ai/regulations/RAI-IT-NA-SUMMARY-2026)). The Garante also recommends recruitment-specific DPIAs addressing algorithmic bias (low confidence) ([PWJennings](https://pwjennings.com/guidance/privacy-law-gdpr-italy-2026)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
The most significant contradiction concerns the compliance deadline: 2 August 2026 versus 2 December 2027, with no clarity on whether the later date reflects adopted law or a proposal. All enforcement-related claims regarding fine amounts, penalty tiers, and the "Omnibus" deferral are below 0.4 confidence and should be treated cautiously. No GDPR enforcement action cited has occurred under the AI Act itself.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether private-sector hiring deployers are legally required to conduct a FRIA; the true legal status of the Omnibus deferral; exact Article 99 penalty tiers; the practical effect of the Commission's missed guidance deadline; how GDPR and AI Act enforcement interact procedurally for hiring tools; and whether any hiring AI systems have completed conformity assessments or registration to date.
